title: Trace Gases, Big Heat
question: How can gases that are a tiny part of the air warm a whole planet?
hook: Carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide together make up less than 0.1% of Earth's air, yet they still produce a greenhouse effect.
idea: Gases whose molecules can interact with infrared radiation absorb the heat Earth's surface gives off, so even small amounts change how warm the planet is.

beats.prompt: Sunlight stays the same, but every greenhouse gas is removed from Earth's air. What happens to the average surface temperature?

choices.label: It stays near 15 °C
choices.feedback: Sunlight is unchanged, but the heat the surface radiates would no longer be absorbed on its way out.

choices.label: It rises, as more sunlight gets through
choices.feedback: Greenhouse gases mainly absorb the heat the surface radiates, so removing them lets heat escape rather than adding warmth.

beats.explain: Sunlight warms the surface, which radiates heat that greenhouse gases mostly absorb; without them Earth would average about −18 °C instead of 15 °C.

beats.prompt: Sort each gas by how it handles the heat Earth radiates.
beats.explain: Molecules made of different elements have an uneven charge that lets them interact with infrared radiation, while single-atom argon lets thermal radiation pass.

beats.prompt: Match each gas to what is true of it.
pairs: Causes about three-quarters of global warming
Lasts about 12 years in the air
Stays in the air about nine days
beats.explain: Each gas differs in how long it stays in the air and how much warming it drives.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the recent rise of greenhouse gases in order.
items: CO₂ has climbed its first 30 ppm
CO₂ has climbed a further 90 ppm
beats.explain: The first 30 ppm rise ran from the Industrial Revolution around 1750 to 1958, the next 90 ppm came by 2014, and warming hit 0.27 °C per decade over 2015–2024.
